analysis.title: Morning Market Tidbits: Adding another hike to our Fed call
key_insights: BofA now expects 25bp Fed hikes at the next three meetings (Dec, Jan, Mar), for a terminal rate of 4.5-4.75%. A Jan '27 hike was added to the prior forecast.
Oct CPI confirmed that the Fed is behind the curve on inflation. BofA says the Fed no longer has the luxury of hiking at a quarterly pace.

Risks to the new Fed call are balanced. The Fed might delay or skip the last hike on a soft patch in the data or a significant tightening in financial conditions. A surge in wage inflation or large annual price resets could push the policy rate above 5%.

A 50bp hike in Dec is not BofA's base case. It would require most or all of: Oct core PCE near 40bp, a 4.0% unemployment rate in Nov, 0.4% wage inflation in Nov, signs that other FOMC participants (particularly the doves) back 50bp, and market pricing of at least a 50% chance of 50bp.
Markets are pricing nearly 50bp of hikes over the next two meetings, per the chart of market pricing by meeting.
BofA's 3Q GDP tracking estimate is unchanged at 3.9% q/q saar after Oct existing home sales, against an official BofA 3Q forecast of 3.4%.
Today's calendar: Oct PPI at 8:30 plus remarks from Fed officials Jefferson, Logan, Bowman, Collins and Daly.

macro_indicators.interpretation: Three consecutive 25bp hikes (Dec, Jan, Mar) are expected, with the Fed hiking at consecutive meetings rather than quarterly.
BofA base case. A 50bp hike is possible but would need nearly everything to break the hawks' way.

tension_points.theme: Fed hike pace and terminal rate
tension_points.bull_case: Hawkish read: Oct CPI shows the Fed behind the curve, so BofA expects 25bp hikes in Dec, Jan and Mar to a terminal rate of 4.5-4.75%, and a 50bp Dec hike is possible if the data and FOMC doves line up.
tension_points.bear_case: The Fed might delay or skip the last hike if there is a soft patch in the data or significant tightening in financial conditions.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A soft patch in the data or significant tightening in financial conditions would lead the Fed to delay or skip the last hike. A surge in wage inflation or large annual price resets could push the rate above 5%.
